result.summary: Hesiod tells the myth of the five ages of men: golden, silver, bronze, heroic and iron. He laments living in the iron age, predicts its moral collapse, and then tells the fable of the hawk and the nightingale to warn princes that might is not right.

scenes.title: The Golden Race
scenes.summary: The gods make a golden race under Cronos who live without toil or sorrow and die as if falling asleep.

place.name: the earth in the time of Cronos

scenes.title: The Silver Race
scenes.summary: A lesser silver race stays childish for a hundred years, then sins and refuses to honour the gods, so Zeus removes them.
scenes.stakes: The silver race is destroyed by Zeus for neglecting the gods.

scenes.title: The Bronze Race
scenes.summary: Zeus makes a violent bronze race from ash-trees; they destroy one another and go to Hades.
scenes.stakes: The bronze race perishes by its own violence and is forgotten.

scenes.title: The Heroes
scenes.summary: The nobler race of heroes dies at Thebes and Troy, or goes to the islands of the blessed where Cronos rules. Zeus then makes a fifth generation.
scenes.stakes: Heroes face death in war, or else a blessed afterlife.

scenes.title: The Iron Age Lament
scenes.summary: Hesiod wishes he were not of the iron race, foretelling family strife, injustice and the departure of Aidos and Nemesis.
scenes.stakes: Mankind faces moral collapse and abandonment by the gods' help.

scenes.title: The Hawk and the Nightingale
scenes.summary: A hawk, carrying a nightingale in his talons, mocks her and says it is foolish to resist the stronger.
scenes.stakes: The nightingale may be eaten or released at the hawk's whim.

notable_quotes.reason: Hesiod's famous wish to have lived in another age.
Moral of the fable: resisting the stronger is folly.
Captures the iron age's collapse of justice: strength becomes right.

analysis.text: The five ages show steady moral decline from golden ease to iron toil, with justice and respect for the gods as the measure of each race.
The myth likely blends Near Eastern ideas of metallic ages with Greek heroic tradition; the heroes alone break the pattern of decline.

legacy.text: The five ages shaped later ideas of a lost golden age, notably Ovid's Metamorphoses and the phrase 'golden age'.
The hawk and nightingale is often counted among the earliest Greek fables, a forerunner of the Aesopic tradition.

fun_facts.text: The heroic age is the only one not named for a metal, which suggests Hesiod fitted the Homeric heroes into an older scheme of four metals.

language_notes.text: "Sum you up another tale" means to set out another account briefly; Hesiod is moving on from the Prometheus and Pandora story.
"Miserable age" is wretched old age, personified as something that did not settle on these men.
"Pure spirits" translates daimones, divine beings between gods and men, here acting as guardians of humans.
"An hundred years" means the silver child stayed a childish simpleton for a century, which marks the race as inferior.
Ash-trees: the bronze men are said to spring from ash trees, perhaps from the wood of spears. The "1304" is a stray footnote marker.
"Adamant" is an unbreakable, legendary hard substance, here a figure for the men's pitiless hearts.
"Ate no bread" means they did not eat grain, the food of civilised men, and so lived by meat and violence.
"Dank" means damp and gloomy; it describes the house of Hades, the underworld.
The flocks of Oedipus refers to the war of the Seven against Thebes, fought over Oedipus' inheritance; Thebe is Thebes, in the land of Cadmus, its founder.
Helen's sake: the Trojan War began when Helen, wife of Menelaus, was taken to Troy by Paris.
Cronos was freed from his bonds by Zeus, who had earlier overthrown him; he now rules the blessed in the islands.
"Would that I were not" is an archaic wish: Hesiod wishes he had died earlier or been born later.
"Might shall be their right" means that whoever has power will decide what counts as justice.
Aidos means shame or reverence; Nemesis means righteous indignation at wrongdoing. Together they restrain human wickedness.

context_notes.text: Cronos ruled the gods before his son Zeus overthrew him. His reign is remembered as a time of ease and plenty.
Zeus, son of Cronos, is king of the gods and enforcer of justice. He punishes those who neglect proper worship.
Ares is the god of war, associated with bloodshed and brutality rather than skill.
Hesiod inserts the Age of Heroes between the Bronze and Iron ages. These heroes are the figures of epic such as those at Thebes and Troy.
The islands of the blessed are a paradise at the world's edge where favoured heroes live after death.
Hesiod addresses the kings (princes) who judge disputes; this fable is his warning about their abuse of power.

literary_notes.text: Death is compared to being overcome by sleep, which makes the golden race's end gentle and untroubled.
Repeating "bronze" for armour, houses and tools stresses a hard, warlike world, with iron not yet known.
These terrifying warriors are brought down by their own hands, and "left no name", so their power ends in oblivion.
Honey-sweet fruit three times a year paints a vivid picture of ease and abundance, contrasting with the toil of the iron race.
Labour by day and perishing by night balances two torments, showing a life with no rest.
Aidos and Nemesis are shown as white-robed figures who leave earth, making the loss of moral restraint tangible.
The hawk and nightingale fable stands for the powerful ruler and the weak victim, perhaps the poet himself.
The hawk's moral that resistance is foolish expresses the very might-is-right attitude Hesiod condemns.
